doctrines.name: Judicial Review
doctrines.subject: Constitutional Law
doctrines.description: The power of courts to review legislative and executive action against the Constitution and declare it invalid. Established in Marbury v. Madison, it is the cornerstone of American constitutional law.

cases.name: Marbury v. Madison
cases.holding: The Supreme Court has the power to review acts of Congress and declare them unconstitutional; Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789, which purported to expand the Court's original jurisdiction, was unconstitutional.

doctrines.name: Federalism & Implied Powers
doctrines.subject: Constitutional Law
doctrines.description: The relationship between the national government and the states, including Congress's implied powers under the Necessary and Proper Clause and the supremacy of federal law.

cases.name: McCulloch v. Maryland
cases.holding: Congress may charter a national bank under the Necessary and Proper Clause, and states may not tax federal instrumentalities: the power to tax involves the power to destroy.

doctrines.name: Commerce Clause
doctrines.subject: Constitutional Law
doctrines.description: Congress's power to regulate interstate commerce, its expansion over 200 years, and the modern limits placed on it. Traces the arc from Gibbons to Wickard and back to Lopez.

cases.name: Gibbons v. Ogden
cases.holding: Interstate commerce includes navigation, and the federal Commerce Clause power is broad — states cannot monopolize steamboat traffic on interstate waterways.

cases.name: Wickard v. Filburn
cases.holding: Congress may regulate purely local activity that, in the aggregate, substantially affects interstate commerce — wheat grown for home consumption.

cases.name: United States v. Lopez
cases.holding: The Gun-Free School Zones Act exceeds the Commerce Clause; Congress cannot regulate non-economic activity with no substantial effect on interstate commerce — the first limit on the clause since 1937.

doctrines.name: Anti-Commandeering
doctrines.subject: Constitutional Law
doctrines.description: The principle that Congress may not commandeer state legislatures or state executives to implement federal regulatory programs, preserving the dual-sovereignty structure of federalism.

cases.name: New York v. United States
cases.holding: Congress may not commandeer state legislatures to enact a federal regulatory program; the 'take title' provision of the Low-Level Radioactive Waste Act violated the Tenth Amendment.

doctrines.name: Separation of Powers
doctrines.subject: Constitutional Law
doctrines.description: The allocation of power among the legislative, executive, and judicial branches, including the limits of executive authority and the qualified nature of executive privilege.

cases.name: Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer
cases.holding: The President cannot seize private steel mills without congressional authorization; Justice Jackson's tripartite framework governs the scope of executive power.

cases.name: United States v. Nixon
cases.holding: Executive privilege is qualified, not absolute; the President must comply with a subpoena in a criminal case because the judiciary is the final arbiter of the Constitution.

doctrines.name: Administrative Deference
doctrines.subject: Administrative Law
doctrines.description: How courts review agency interpretations of statutes. The two-step Chevron framework dominated administrative law for four decades before being overruled in 2024.

cases.name: Chevron v. NRDC
cases.holding: Courts should defer to reasonable agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes at Chevron step two — a doctrine overruled by Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024).

doctrines.name: Equal Protection
doctrines.subject: Constitutional Law
doctrines.description: The Fourteenth Amendment's guarantee of equal protection of the laws — from Plessy's separate-but-equal to Brown, the tiers of scrutiny, and the modern doctrine of race-conscious classifications.

cases.name: Plessy v. Ferguson
cases.holding: Separate but equal railway accommodations do not violate the Equal Protection Clause — overruled by Brown v. Board of Education (1954).

cases.name: United States v. Carolene Products Co.
cases.holding: Economic regulation is reviewed under rational basis; Footnote 4 suggested heightened scrutiny for 'discrete and insular minorities' — the origin of the tiers of scrutiny.

cases.name: Brown v. Board of Education
cases.holding: Racial segregation in public schools violates the Equal Protection Clause; separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.

cases.name: Loving v. Virginia
cases.holding: Racial restrictions on marriage violate both the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment.

cases.name: Korematsu v. United States
cases.holding: The wartime exclusion of Japanese Americans was upheld under military necessity — a decision widely discredited and repudiated in Trump v. Hawaii (2018).

cases.name: Grutter v. Bollinger
cases.holding: Narrowly tailored affirmative action in law school admissions survives strict scrutiny because student-body diversity is a compelling state interest — later limited by Students for Fair Admissions (2023).

doctrines.name: Voting Rights & Apportionment
doctrines.subject: Constitutional Law
doctrines.description: The constitutional rules governing legislative districts, racial gerrymandering, and the reach of the Voting Rights Act.

cases.name: Baker v. Carr
cases.holding: Equal-protection challenges to legislative apportionment are justiciable; federal courts may hear one-person-one-vote claims.

cases.name: Shaw v. Reno
cases.holding: Racial gerrymandering claims are cognizable under the Equal Protection Clause where a district is so bizarre on its face that it can only be explained by race.

cases.name: Shelby County v. Holder
cases.holding: The preclearance coverage formula of Section 4(b) of the Voting Rights Act violates the Tenth Amendment's equal sovereignty principle; Congress must update it.

doctrines.name: Standing & Justiciability
doctrines.subject: Constitutional Law
doctrines.description: The threshold rules that decide when a case is fit for federal court: standing, ripeness, mootness, and the political question doctrine.

cases.name: Baker v. Carr
cases.holding: Equal-protection challenges to legislative apportionment are justiciable; federal courts may hear one-person-one-vote claims.

cases.name: Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife
cases.holding: Standing requires an injury in fact, a causal connection, and redressability; Congress cannot erase the Article III case-or-controversy requirement.

doctrines.name: Substantive Due Process & Privacy
doctrines.subject: Constitutional Law
doctrines.description: The contested doctrine that the Due Process Clauses protect unenumerated fundamental rights — contraception, marriage, intimacy, and abortion — and the modern battle over its scope.

cases.name: Griswold v. Connecticut
cases.holding: The Constitution protects marital privacy through the penumbras and emanations of the Bill of Rights; a ban on contraceptives for married couples is unconstitutional.

cases.name: Roe v. Wade
cases.holding: The right of privacy under the Due Process Clause includes a woman's decision to terminate a pregnancy under the trimester framework — overruled by Dobbs v. Jackson (2022).

cases.name: Lawrence v. Texas
cases.holding: Criminalizing same-sex sexual intimacy violates the Due Process Clause; Bowers v. Hardwick is overruled.

cases.name: Obergefell v. Hodges
cases.holding: The Fourteenth Amendment requires states to both license and recognize same-sex marriages; the right to marry is fundamental.

cases.name: Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health
cases.holding: The Constitution does not confer a right to abortion; Roe and Casey are overruled, returning abortion regulation to the states.

doctrines.name: Privileges or Immunities
doctrines.subject: Constitutional Law
doctrines.description: The Fourteenth Amendment's Privileges or Immunities Clause, narrowly read since 1873 to protect only federal citizenship rights — one of the great 'paths not taken' in constitutional law.

cases.name: Slaughter-House Cases
cases.holding: The Privileges or Immunities Clause protects only the privileges of federal citizenship, not state citizenship — a narrow reading that channeled rights claims through the Due Process Clause instead.

doctrines.name: Free Speech & Press
doctrines.subject: First Amendment
doctrines.description: The core First Amendment doctrines: incitement, defamation, obscenity, expressive conduct, and student speech. Traces the evolution from the clear-and-present-danger test to modern categorical rules.

cases.name: Schenck v. United States
cases.holding: Speech may be punished when it creates a clear and present danger of the evils Congress may prevent — the test later replaced by Brandenburg's imminent lawless action.

cases.name: New York Times v. Sullivan
cases.holding: Public officials must prove actual malice — knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth — to win a defamation suit.

cases.name: Miller v. California
cases.holding: Obscenity is defined by the three-part Miller test (prurient interest, patently offensive, serious value) and falls outside First Amendment protection.

cases.name: Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District
cases.holding: Students retain First Amendment rights in school unless their speech substantially and materially disrupts the educational process.

cases.name: Brandenburg v. Ohio
cases.holding: Speech advocating lawlessness is protected unless it is directed to inciting and likely to incite imminent lawless action.

cases.name: Texas v. Johnson
cases.holding: Burning the American flag is expressive conduct protected by the First Amendment; the government cannot ban it to preserve the flag's symbolic value.

cases.name: New York Times v. United States
cases.holding: The government bears a heavy presumption against prior restraint; the Pentagon Papers could not be enjoined without proof of direct national-security harm.

doctrines.name: Prior Restraint
doctrines.subject: First Amendment
doctrines.description: The doctrine that government may not restrain speech before it occurs, except in the most exceptional circumstances — from Near's newspapers to the Pentagon Papers.

cases.name: Near v. Minnesota
cases.holding: Prior restraint is presumptively unconstitutional and applies to the states via the Fourteenth Amendment; a gag order on a defamatory newspaper was invalid.

cases.name: New York Times v. United States
cases.holding: The government bears a heavy presumption against prior restraint; the Pentagon Papers could not be enjoined without proof of direct national-security harm.

doctrines.name: Religious Freedom
doctrines.subject: First Amendment
doctrines.description: The Free Exercise and Establishment Clauses: when generally applicable laws may burden religion, the Amish exemption, and the rise and fall of the Lemon test.

cases.name: Wisconsin v. Yoder
cases.holding: Compulsory school attendance beyond eighth grade violates the Amish's Free Exercise rights where it threatens their religious way of life.

cases.name: Lemon v. Kurtzman
cases.holding: The Establishment Clause requires the three-part Lemon test (secular purpose, no primary religious effect, no excessive entanglement) — a framework later widely disfavored and effectively abandoned.

cases.name: Employment Division v. Smith
cases.holding: Neutral, generally applicable laws that burden religious exercise do not violate the Free Exercise Clause; strict scrutiny is not required — partially superseded by the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (1993).

doctrines.name: Commercial Speech & Campaign Finance
doctrines.subject: First Amendment
doctrines.description: The intermediate scrutiny applied to advertising and the First Amendment limits on regulating money in politics — from the Buckley distinction to corporate speech in Citizens United.

cases.name: Buckley v. Valeo
cases.holding: Campaign expenditure limits violate the First Amendment, but contribution limits are upheld — creating the spending/contributions distinction that still governs campaign finance.

cases.name: Central Hudson Gas & Electric Corp. v. Public Service Commission
cases.holding: Commercial speech receives intermediate scrutiny under the four-part Central Hudson test (lawful activity, substantial government interest, direct advancement, narrow tailoring).

cases.name: Citizens United v. FEC
cases.holding: Corporate independent expenditures in elections are protected political speech; the BCRA's electioneering-communication ban is unconstitutional.

doctrines.name: Second Amendment
doctrines.subject: Constitutional Law
doctrines.description: The modern individual-rights reading of the right to keep and bear arms, announced in Heller after nearly 70 years of silence on the subject.

cases.name: District of Columbia v. Heller
cases.holding: The Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep and bear arms for self-defense in the home; the District's handgun ban is unconstitutional.

doctrines.name: Search & Seizure
doctrines.subject: Criminal Procedure
doctrines.description: Fourth Amendment doctrine: the exclusionary rule, the reasonable-expectation-of-privacy test, stop and frisk, and the wingspan limit on searches incident to arrest.

cases.name: Mapp v. Ohio
cases.holding: The exclusionary rule applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment; evidence seized in violation of the Fourth Amendment is inadmissible.

cases.name: Katz v. United States
cases.holding: The Fourth Amendment protects people, not places; wiretapping a phone booth without a warrant violates a reasonable expectation of privacy.

cases.name: Terry v. Ohio
cases.holding: A brief investigatory stop and frisk for weapons is permitted on reasonable suspicion of criminal activity, weighing crime prevention against the Fourth Amendment.

cases.name: Chimel v. California
cases.holding: A search incident to arrest is limited to the area within the arrestee's immediate control; the full-house search was unconstitutional.

doctrines.name: Self-Incrimination & Miranda
doctrines.subject: Criminal Procedure
doctrines.description: The Fifth Amendment right against compelled self-incrimination and the Miranda warning regime that guards it in custodial interrogation.

cases.name: Miranda v. Arizona
cases.holding: Suspects in custody must be warned of their right to remain silent and to counsel before interrogation; statements obtained without warnings are inadmissible.

doctrines.name: Right to Counsel & Fair Trial
doctrines.subject: Criminal Procedure
doctrines.description: The Sixth and Fourteenth Amendment guarantees of counsel and the prosecutor's duty to disclose exculpatory evidence — twin pillars of a fair trial.

cases.name: Brady v. Maryland
cases.holding: The prosecution must disclose material exculpatory evidence to the defense, or the conviction is unconstitutional — the foundation of the Brady disclosure rule.

cases.name: Gideon v. Wainwright
cases.holding: The Sixth Amendment right to counsel applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment; states must provide counsel to indigent felony defendants.

doctrines.name: Jury Selection & Equal Protection
doctrines.subject: Criminal Procedure
doctrines.description: The constitutional limit on peremptory strikes: prosecutors (and in later cases, criminal defendants) may not exclude jurors on the basis of race.

cases.name: Batson v. Kentucky
cases.holding: Peremptory strikes exercised on the basis of race violate the Equal Protection Clause; a defendant can challenge them under the Batson three-step inquiry.

doctrines.name: Cruel & Unusual Punishment
doctrines.subject: Criminal Procedure
doctrines.description: The Eighth Amendment's prohibition on cruel and unusual punishments, applied to the death penalty's arbitrary administration.

cases.name: Furman v. Georgia
cases.holding: The death penalty as administered was arbitrary and discriminatory, violating the Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause — a moratorium that states later reformed around (Gregg v. Georgia, 1976).

doctrines.name: Consideration
doctrines.subject: Contracts
doctrines.description: The bargain element that makes a promise enforceable: what counts as consideration, including forbearance of a legal right.

cases.name: Hamer v. Sidway
cases.holding: Forbearance of a legal right — an uncle's promise not to drink or gamble in exchange for the nephew's abstinence — constitutes valid consideration.

doctrines.name: Formation & Unconscionability
doctrines.subject: Contracts
doctrines.description: When a contract is formed (objective intent) and when courts will refuse to enforce it (unconscionability).

cases.name: Lucy v. Zehmer
cases.holding: Contractual intent is judged by objective manifestations; a signed agreement to sell a farm is enforceable even where a party claims it was made in jest.

cases.name: Williams v. Walker-Thomas Furniture Co.
cases.holding: A court may refuse to enforce a contract for unconscionability where grossly unfair terms and unequal bargaining power shock the conscience.

doctrines.name: Damages & Expectancy
doctrines.subject: Contracts
doctrines.description: How contract damages are measured: expectation damages that put the promisee in the position promised, limited by foreseeability at formation.

cases.name: Hadley v. Baxendale
cases.holding: Consequential damages are recoverable only for losses within the parties' reasonable contemplation at the time of contract formation — the famous foreseeability rule.

cases.name: Hawkins v. McGee
cases.holding: Expectation damages give the plaintiff the benefit of the bargain — the 'hairy hand' case, where damages were measured by the perfect hand promised, not the cost of surgery.

doctrines.name: Negligence & Duty
doctrines.subject: Torts
doctrines.description: The fault-based liability regime: the ordinary-care standard, the duty of care owed to foreseeable plaintiffs, manufacturer liability without privity, and the Hand formula.

cases.name: Brown v. Kendall
cases.holding: Accidental injuries require proof of fault; liability rests on a failure to exercise ordinary care, not on strict liability for the act.

cases.name: MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co.
cases.holding: Manufacturers owe a duty of care to ultimate consumers even without privity of contract; Buick was liable for the defective wheel that injured a remote buyer.

cases.name: Palsgraf v. Long Island Railroad
cases.holding: A duty of care runs only to foreseeable plaintiffs; the railroad owed no duty to Mrs. Palsgraf because her injury was an unforeseeable consequence of its conduct.

cases.name: United States v. Carroll Towing Co.
cases.holding: Negligence is determined by the Hand formula: a duty of care is breached where the burden of adequate precautions is less than the probability of harm times its severity (B < PL).

doctrines.name: Strict Liability
doctrines.subject: Torts
doctrines.description: Liability without fault for abnormally dangerous activities and defective products — the escape of dangerous things and the emerging doctrine of strict products liability.

cases.name: Rylands v. Fletcher
cases.holding: A landowner is strictly liable for the escape of dangerous things brought onto land for non-natural uses — here, water flooding a neighbor's mine.

cases.name: Escola v. Coca Cola Bottling Co.
cases.holding: Res ipsa loquitur applies to an exploding soda bottle; Justice Traynor's concurrence argued for strict products liability because manufacturers can bear and spread the cost of harm.

doctrines.name: Acquisition & Sovereignty
doctrines.subject: Property
doctrines.description: How property rights come into being: first possession of wild animals and the discovery doctrine's impact on Native American land title.

cases.name: Pierson v. Post
cases.holding: First possession of a wild animal requires actual capture or control, not mere pursuit — the fox case that fixed the capture rule.

cases.name: Johnson v. M'Intosh
cases.holding: Under the discovery doctrine, European sovereigns acquired title to discovered lands; Native American tribes retain only a right of occupancy — a doctrine later repudiated in federal Indian law.

doctrines.name: Takings & Public Use
doctrines.subject: Property
doctrines.description: The Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause: when regulations go so far as to effect a taking, and what counts as public use in eminent domain.

cases.name: Penn Central Transportation Co. v. New York City
cases.holding: Regulatory takings are judged by an ad hoc multifactor test (economic impact, interference with investment-backed expectations, character of the action); the Grand Central landmark law was not a taking.

cases.name: Kelo v. City of New London
cases.holding: 'Public use' under the Takings Clause includes economic development by a private developer, so long as just compensation is paid — one of the most controversial eminent-domain decisions.

doctrines.name: Property Rights & Their Limits
doctrines.subject: Property
doctrines.description: The principle that property rights are not absolute: an owner's right to exclude yields to the public interest and the basic needs of those on the land.

cases.name: State v. Shack
cases.holding: A landowner may not exclude government officials entering to provide essential services to migrant farmworkers; property rights do not include absolute dominion.

doctrines.name: Personal Jurisdiction
doctrines.subject: Civil Procedure
doctrines.description: The constitutional limits on a court's power over defendants — from physical presence in Pennoyer to minimum contacts and purposeful availment in the modern era.

cases.name: Pennoyer v. Neff
cases.holding: A court has personal jurisdiction over a defendant only through presence within the forum or consent; in rem jurisdiction attaches to property in the state.

cases.name: International Shoe Co. v. Washington
cases.holding: Personal jurisdiction requires minimum contacts such that the suit does not offend traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice.

cases.name: Asahi Metal Industry Co. v. Superior Court
cases.holding: Mere placement of a product into the stream of commerce is insufficient for jurisdiction; the exercise of jurisdiction must be reasonable and comport with fair play.

doctrines.name: Erie Doctrine & Pleading
doctrines.subject: Civil Procedure
doctrines.description: The two great structural rules of modern federal civil litigation: state law governs substantive issues in diversity, and pleadings must state a plausible claim.

cases.name: Erie Railroad v. Tompkins
cases.holding: Federal courts sitting in diversity must apply state substantive law; there is no general federal common law — Swift v. Tyson is overruled.

cases.name: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
cases.holding: Complaints must plead a facially plausible claim, not merely a conceivable one — the Twombly/Iqbal plausibility standard that governs federal pleading.
